briefing.text: The bh35 tables (clinical patient and sample files, gene panel matrix, mutations) describe a breast cancer whole-exome cohort. The library expects them to hold no fusion or structural-variant calls, no AKT3 fusion rows and no drug-response variable. Check this yourself: look at Variant_Classification values and at AKT3/MAGI3 rows in data_mutations.txt, and at every clinical column. Under the benchmark convention, a hypothesis about this study's cancer type and genes gets True or False even when the measurement it needs (fusion calls, inhibitor experiments) was not deposited. A missing variable alone does not justify 'Not verifiable'.
briefing.reason: The obvious mistake here is to answer 'Not verifiable' because the tables have no fusion or drug data. The team needs to decide whether the hypothesis belongs to this study before choosing a label.

briefing.text: Do not treat ATP-competitive and allosteric AKT inhibitors as the same. ATP-competitive inhibitors (e.g. GSK690693, ipatasertib, capivasertib) bind the ATP pocket in the kinase domain. Allosteric inhibitors (e.g. MK-2206) need the PH domain to hold AKT in its inactive conformation. The library reports, from domain knowledge it could not check, that MAGI3-AKT3 fusions keep the AKT3 kinase domain and lose the PH domain, which makes them PIP3-independent and constitutively active. Base the mechanistic argument on whether this inhibitor class's binding site survives in the fusion, not on generic 'AKT inhibitor resistance'.
briefing.reason: The data cannot test the claim directly, so the label must come from biology. Mixing up the two inhibitor classes would lead to the wrong mechanistic conclusion.

briefing.text: Library note, from domain knowledge only (web unavailable, medium confidence, no sources): ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors are generally expected to keep their activity against AKT variants that lack the PH domain, because their binding site is in the kinase domain. Allosteric PH-dependent inhibitors such as MK-2206 are expected to lose activity against PH-deleted AKT. Weigh this as an expert prior to be checked against your own knowledge of AKT pharmacology.
briefing.reason: This is the key pharmacological premise for any reasoning from established biology. It is passed down with its unverified status stated, so the team can judge it rather than simply accept it.

briefing.text: When direct testing is impossible, compare the hypothesis's absolute wording ('cannot be abolished') with what the study that produced this cohort most likely reported about the fusion and ATP-competitive AKT inhibition. Under the benchmark convention, a hypothesis may be the study's finding or that finding reversed.
briefing.reason: Under the labelling convention, the label depends on whether the claim matches or reverses the source study's finding. Absolute wording is often the sign of a reversal.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume the hypothesis is a reversal of a finding of this breast WXS study (Mexico/Vietnam cohort) and not a claim imported from another publication, so 'Not verifiable' is ruled out.
Both assume the fusion keeps the AKT3 kinase domain (ATP-binding pocket) so an ATP-competitive inhibitor should act on it; neither checked this against the data, which cannot show it anyway.
unused_evidence: Neither team used the Somatic Status, Purity/Ploidy or TMB columns; none of these measures fusion or drug response, so ignoring them is unlikely to change the label.
Team B did not report a receptor/PAM50 check; team A did (11 triple-negative, 13 Basal), which ties the cohort to the subtype in which the fusion was reported.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named the same weak point: the label rests on recalled study findings and kinase pharmacology, not on table data. This is unavoidable under the benchmark convention, and neither team resolved it beyond reporting it.
second_readings: 'Cannot be abolished' could be read as 'is not fully abolished' (partial inhibition), and that reading would favour True only if the study reported residual activity. Both teams read the study as reporting that activation was abolished, so the absolute wording is the reversed form.
challenge.verdict: High trust in the agreed label. The cohort clearly matches the study that reported this fusion, the label rests on that study's reported pharmacology, and I found no plausible second reading or unused data field that could change it.

In general, do ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors (as opposed to allosteric PH-domain-dependent inhibitors) still inhibit AKT fusion proteins that lose the PH domain but keep the kinase domain?
questions.why: Neither team verified which inhibitor class depends on which domain, and that is the mechanistic basis both labels rest on.

findings.question: In general, do ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors (as opposed to allosteric PH-domain-dependent inhibitors) still inhibit AKT fusion proteins that lose the PH domain but keep the kinase domain?
findings.answer: Not settled from the web: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on all 3 calls (2 searches and 1 contents call), so no page was read. From domain knowledge only, not verified: yes. ATP-competitive inhibitors (GSK690693, ipatasertib, capivasertib, AZD5363) bind the ATP pocket in the kinase domain, which the fusion keeps, so they are expected to still inhibit PH-less AKT fusions such as MAGI3-AKT3. Allosteric inhibitors (MK-2206, Akti-1/2) need the PH-domain/kinase-domain interface and are expected to lose activity. On this basis, the claim that an ATP-competitive inhibitor cannot abolish MAGI3-AKT3 activity goes against the expected pharmacology.
